#9817. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

A local model can manage a brief question without any issues, but it may have difficulty when dealing with a complete document. The model's internal settings stay the same, but the effort needed and the memory required to process the request increase a lot.

In Part 1, I explained how to run a quantized model on a smaller GPU.

The next step is to choose a task, measure how long it takes, and find a setup that works within the GPU's limits.

This guide uses Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct along with llama.cpp.

It includes memory calculations, a fixed starting configuration, and a Python-based benchmark that you can run on your own computer. The numerical memory estimates are calculated values, and this article does not claim to have measured improvements in GPU performance.

To understand the actual delay you experience, there are two main waiting periods in a conversation. The first occurs when the model processes the initial prompt, often called the prefill phase. The second happens when the model generates the answer one word at a time, known as the decode phase.

If a document takes several seconds to process, fast decoding won't eliminate that initial delay. However, if the first words appear quickly but the rest of the response is slow, then the decoding phase is the area that needs optimization.

Delay before the client receives the first nonempty text chunk

Whether two runs produced comparable amounts of text

A target such as "start a short answer within two seconds" can guide your own experiments. It is a product requirement you choose, not a promised result for every 8GB card.

The model file is only part of the memory requirement. During generation, the runtime also stores attention keys and values for tokens already processed. This KV cache avoids recomputing those states, but it needs memory of its own. Working buffers and other GPU applications need space too. [1]

For a conventional full-attention transformer, an approximate KV-cache payload is:

KV bytes = 2 x layers x stored tokens x KV heads x head dimension

The initial 2 accounts for keys and values. Use the number of KV heads, which can differ from the number of query heads.

Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct has 28 layers, 4 KV heads, and a head dimension of 128, obtained from its hidden size of 3,584 divided by 28 query heads. With FP16 cache elements, the calculation becomes 2 x 28 x tokens x 4 x 128 x 2. [2]

These figures describe one sequence and exclude allocation padding, runtime buffers, and model weights. They are not measurements of total VRAM usage. Other architectures, cache layouts, and attention types need different calculations.

This is why a large advertised context window needs its own memory budget. On this model, moving from 4K to 32K tokens adds about 1.53 GiB of calculated FP16 cache payload. Whether that increase fits depends on everything else already occupying the GPU.

Weight quantization and cache quantization are separate choices. A Q4_K_M model can still use an FP16 KV cache. Reducing cache precision may free up space, but it needs a quality check and a latency measurement. Hugging Face's cache documentation also cautions that cache quantization can hurt latency in some short-context situations. [1]

The shell commands below target Linux or WSL2 with an NVIDIA GPU. Install a working NVIDIA driver, a compatible CUDA Toolkit, Git, CMake, and a C++ compiler first. The benchmark itself requires Python 3.10 or newer and no third-party Python packages.

Use the current CMake build route in the llama.cpp build documentation: [3]

Keep that checkout unchanged throughout the experiment. Save the model filenames and their SHA-256 hashes too, including every shard if the download is split. A model tag alone is not enough to reproduce an experiment after its files change.

I use the official Qwen GGUF repository because its model configuration is available to inspect. It is a concrete baseline, not a claim that this is the best available model. [4]

Start the server from the llama.cpp directory:

The first launch downloads the selected model. Exclude that download and startup from request timings. Once the server is ready, inspect its log for the CUDA device, layer placement, cache allocation, and effective context settings. If an installed version rejects an option, consult its saved help output before continuing. The current server options are documented upstream. [5]

This configuration requests full GPU offload; it does not guarantee that every 8GB system has enough free memory. If startup fails, first close another GPU workload or test a smaller context. If partial offload is necessary, record the actual GPU layer count and use it consistently across the comparison.

The baseline has one request slot. Keep other inference clients stopped while measuring. With automatic fitting disabled, a failed configuration is visible instead of becoming a different experiment through an adjusted setting.

Project Cedar: Mira owns the CSV import validator.

Duplicate IDs are blocking the import test.

In at most 80 words, identify the owner, target date, and blocker. Then say whether the notes contain an approved budget amount. Do not invent missing details. Save the following script as bench_local.py. It formats the prompt using the server's chat template, checks a declared token budget, performs a warm-up, and records five measured requests by default.

In a second terminal, run it from the folder containing the script and input:

Its ttft_s is a client-side approximation of time to first token: timing starts before the generation HTTP request and stops at the first nonempty content chunk. That chunk may contain more than one token. Template formatting, token counting, model loading, and any document retrieval happen outside this timer.

The script uses the server's token statistics for decoding speed. Counting streaming events would measure chunks, whose boundaries are not reliable token boundaries. The native completion endpoint and its timing fields are documented in llama.cpp. [5]

Prefix reuse is disabled for these comparisons. The model still uses a KV cache within each generation; the setting prevents an identical prompt from being accelerated by a previous request's prefix. The separate warm-up is excluded from the median. Failed or truncated requests stop the experiment instead of producing a successful-looking score.

The --context value is a declared budget, not a command that reconfigures the server. Match it to the server's effective context. The script allows an additional 32-token reserve and records the formatted input token count.

Repeat the test with a realistic document saved in another input file. Keep that file unchanged across configurations. A short fixture helps check the pipeline, but it cannot establish long-document performance.

Restart the server for each configuration, adjusting only the settings listed here. Everything else, including weights, prompt files, output cap, and GPU placement, stays fixed.

A to B tests Flash Attention. B to C tests cache precision. C to D tests the larger context allocation. D to E tests a larger physical batch. Q8_0 cache support depends on the model, backend, and build; inspect startup output and skip unsupported combinations rather than comparing a fallback unknowingly. [5]

For C, replace the baseline attention and cache options with:

Flash Attention is designed to reduce memory traffic during attention computation. It does not remove the persistent KV-cache requirement. [6] A larger physical batch may help prompt processing but can require more temporary memory, so treat E as an experiment rather than a recommended default.

There are two different comparisons to make. Use the same input across A through E to compare configuration overhead. Separately, increase the actual input length to study longer requests. Changing an 8K capacity setting while keeping a 200-token prompt does not simulate an 8K prompt.

Monitor GPU usage in a third terminal: [7]

Stop sampling with Ctrl+C when the experiment ends. These are device-wide samples, including other processes; one-second sampling can miss brief peaks. Use them alongside the server's allocation logs, not as an exact per-request peak measurement.

Compare median first-text delay, decoding rate, total time, and the observed range. Also inspect output lengths and stop_type: an answer that hit the output limit may be incomplete. Five repetitions are an initial check, not enough evidence for a dependable p95 latency claim.

For the Cedar fixture, check that the answer preserves Mira, the date, and duplicate IDs. It should also distinguish an unapproved budget from a known budget amount. A faster configuration that invents an amount fails this task.

Build a small fixed test set from the work you intend to do. Include a question answered by a detail near the end of a document, an extraction task with a required format, and a question whose answer is absent. Save the generated text before changing cache precision or switching to a smaller model.

A useful score is the number of tasks that meet your written acceptance rules. Keep those rules unchanged while comparing settings. Temperature zero reduces sampling variation, but numerical differences across backends and builds can still affect output.

Once the runtime is measured, inspect what the application sends it. A chat assistant can accumulate old turns, repeated instructions, and irrelevant document chunks until most of its context carries little useful evidence.

For a document assistant with a 4,096-token context, this is one possible allocation:

These are application design choices, not model limits or measured token counts. Count the fully formatted prompt with the model's tokenizer. The input and reserved output must fit together.

Remove duplicate excerpts and retain passages that support the answer, including qualifications and conflicting evidence. Evaluate retrieval changes against the fixed question set. A shorter prompt is only useful when it still contains what the model needs. Once a configuration meets your latency target and quality checks, save its launch command, engine revision, model hashes, prompts, raw responses, and GPU logs together. That gives you a working profile you can revisit when a model update or a new workload changes the results.

[1] Hugging Face Transformers, Cache strategies.

[2] Qwen, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct configuration. The KV-cache table is calculated from these architecture values.

[4] Qwen, Official Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct GGUF repository.

[5] llama.cpp, HTTP server documentation.

[7] NVIDIA, NVIDIA System Management Interface documentation.

#9814. AI Agent Memory (Part 1): Why Remembering Isn't the Same as Learning

I'm ShaoTung Lien (練紹彤). I translate complex business requirements into practical Cloud and AI architecture decisions, focusing on enterpris

I'm ShaoTung Lien (練紹彤). I translate complex business requirements into practical Cloud and AI architecture decisions, focusing on enterpris

I'm ShaoTung Lien (練紹彤). I translate complex business requirements into practical Cloud and AI architecture decisions, focusing on enterpris

AI agents preserve experience in histories, notes, and reusable instructions, then bring it back through search and retrieval. Their models also carry broad knowledge learned during training. But for memory to improve future behavior, it must help a system notice what matters, recognize a situation, and choose an appropriate action.

In Christopher Nolan's Memento, Leonard struggles to form new lasting memories. He uses photographs, notes, and tattoos to work out what happened and what to do next.

The notes help him carry on. But which note does he find? What did it leave out? Does he read it correctly? He can keep a conclusion and lose the reason he trusted it.

That is a useful way to think about agent memory. A deployed language model usually does not change its parameters after each conversation. These are the numerical settings it learned during training. Software around the model saves the history and brings information back when work resumes.

The comparison has limits. The model already knows a lot. It can reason about new information and help check its records. Still, the film gives us a good question: how does yesterday's note help with today's decision?

Working memory helps you keep track of the pan and what to do next.

Episodic memory lets you recall the dinner you burned and what happened that evening.

Semantic memory is general knowledge, such as knowing that thin slices cook quickly.

Procedural memory helps you do things you have practiced, like moving the pan and adjusting the heat without talking yourself through every step.

These functions work together. They are not identical boxes, and a memory does not have to pass through them in order.

An agent's log can help it use a past event. Written instructions can help it carry out a task. But the files alone do not show that it remembers or acts the way a person does.

During training, a model learns language, facts, relationships, and ways to solve problems. That knowledge is spread across its parameters. It is not a library of pages the model searches.

When we use it, we supply context: instructions, conversation, information found through search, and tool results. Examples and corrections in the context can change its answer without changing its parameters.

The agent harness is the software around the model. It manages tools, keeps track of the task, and decides what the model receives next. It can save chats, pull out lessons, find documents, or load a Skill: reusable instructions, sometimes with scripts and supporting files.

This helps. A saved preference can improve tomorrow's answer. A tested script can make a task more reliable. But once a correction leaves context, something has to save it and bring it back when needed.

An experienced cook hears the sizzling change and lowers the heat. A beginner may hear the same sound and miss the warning. Practice helped the cook notice something useful.

We will use a few terms for this throughout the series:

These affect each other. If you expect trouble, you look more closely. If you see something surprising, you may change your expectation.

Human experiments show that past experience can guide attention even when we are not trying to recall it. People still forget and make bad calls. The useful point is that experience can change how we read the next situation.

An agent saves a log, writes a lesson, and stores it. Later, search or a selector chooses what to bring into context. Some guidance is added automatically.

There are several ways this can go wrong. The lesson leaves out an exception. Its description does not match the new task. Or the agent finds the right note, but the situation has changed.

This is where I would look: did yesterday's experience help the agent notice the right thing and make a better choice today?

Memory is what we keep from the past. Learning is how the past changes what we do next.

Useful learning should help later work. Does the agent spot a familiar risk, change an outdated expectation, or choose a method with fewer reminders?

A saved rule, a better selector, or model training could help. External memory also gives us something we can read and correct.

More records alone do not prove competence. I want to see the agent still do the job well when the situation changes, including when an old method should not be used.

The next question is how the system knows which saved lesson matters now.

#9813. Why does my challah have stretch marks?: How to stop your challah from tearing.

Recently, our Community Development Coordinator Kat Mayerovitch shared a very important update from the King Arthur Baking subreddit: a surprising amount of people were wondering why their challah has “stretch marks.”

If you’re not one of those people and don’t know exactly what that means, you may still be familiar with the problem: Sometimes, challah loaves come out of the oven with stretches or tears along the braided strands. It doesn’t affect the quality of the bread, but it does affect the appearance.

To address this issue, I asked our Baking School Curriculum Developer Jack Tissiere for their thoughts on this problem, and they identified two potential causes.

Challah dough rises twice: Once after it’s mixed (known as bulk fermentation) and a second time after the loaf is shaped or braided. Cutting short that second rise can lead to a challah that develops tears as it bakes. As Jack explains, “When we underproof our challah loaves (in other words, don't give them enough time to rise), the bread is still super active and energetic. When it hits the heat of the oven it expands energetically, and that sudden burst of volume before the dough sets can cause the bread to stretch or rip.”

How to fix: Give your braided challah loaf a little more time to rise before baking. Push the proof until the loaf is puffy and marshmallow-y; when you press it with a floured finger, the indent should slowly fill in, which is a sign that it’s ready to be baked. Sometimes, depending on the temperature of both your dough and your environment, this can take longer than the recipe says; trust your instincts rather than relying on the clock. If you fully proof the bread, when you put the loaf into the oven it’s less energetic, which means there isn’t as much oven spring (and subsequent tearing) while baking.

The other reason your challah may have stretch marks is because the loaves are shaped or braided too tightly. As Jack explains “When loaves are braided very tightly, they don’t have a lot of room to grow during the rising and baking process, causing stretches or tears as they expand.”

How to fix: Give your challah dough some slack when shaping: Braid loosely, allowing extra space for the dough to expand as it undergoes its final proof before baking. And for a pretty, even braid, start braiding from the middle; this video shows you how.

Ready to tackle your next braided loaf? Check out our Braided Challah recipe from The Big Book of Bread.

#9811. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9810. We Built a Test to Catch Contact Forms That Lie. It Lied to Us Five Times First

Founder of Formgong, a backend for website forms. I write about why contact forms break and how to test them. formgong.com

Founder of Formgong, a backend for website forms. I write about why contact forms break and how to test them. formgong.com

Founder of Formgong, a backend for website forms. I write about why contact forms break and how to test them. formgong.com

My team builds a form backend, and the most common message we get is some version of "my form stopped working". Usually the form never worked. Someone generated the site, clicked Send once, saw a green "Message sent!" and moved on. In early October we got tired of guessing how often that happens and decided to count it on sites built with Lovable and Bolt.

On paper the plan was short. Open a live site, find the contact form, fill it in with test values nobody would type for real, press Send and watch what leaves the page. If a request goes out with our text in it, the form sends. If nothing goes out and the page still celebrates, the form is fake. Every request after the click was blocked in the browser, so no site owner got a test message from us.

We wrote the rules down before the first site was tested. The test went through 793 sites and found 119 contact forms. It took six runs to get to the final answer, which was 27 fakes out of the 105 forms with a clear result.

Six runs, because the test itself kept getting things wrong. These are the five times it fooled us, more or less in the order we noticed.

Version one counted any request after the click as "the form sent something". If you've ever opened the network tab on a modern landing page, you can guess what happened. Pressing Send also pings Google Analytics, Tag Manager, Clarity, Hotjar, PostHog or Vercel's insights, and Lovable sites call their own analytics endpoint too. A fake form with three trackers on the page passed as a working one.

So "sends" got a stricter meaning. A request only counts if it carries what we typed. We picked test values that stand out, an example.com address and a phone number starting with 555, which made them easy to find in a URL or a request body. Known analytics hosts were ignored on top of that.

During the pilot, one site cleared its fields after Send and that was it. No toast, no text, no request. It looked like a form that simply does nothing. It turned out the site had shown an alert(), and the browser automation had dismissed it before we could read it.

After that, whatever a dialog said was treated as part of the page.

After the full run, we went through the fakes by hand. For each one we opened the site's JavaScript and read the submit handler. Most were exactly what we expected, and the pattern became familiar quickly: wait a second, show a green toast, reset the fields. No fetch, no email service, no database.

But two forms we had confirmed as fake by reading their code were classed as "nothing happened". They showed "Message sent!" for two or three seconds and then hid it. Our test read the page once, five seconds after the click, by which point the toast was gone.

The fix was to sample the page every 250 milliseconds for five seconds and keep every new line of text we saw. In the same pass we found a form that sent people to mailto: by setting location.href. Navigations like that never show up as network requests, so we hooked them separately.

This one is my favourite. A site returned a "queued" message, but its code clearly sent requests. On a closer look, the handler had a honeypot, a hidden field that only bots fill in. If the field has a value, the form quietly shows a fake success and drops the message. Our test filled every text field it could find, including that hidden one, so the site correctly treated us as a bot.

So the test stopped filling fields that a person can't see or reach. That created the next problem.

After that change, three sites that had been sending started refusing our test values. We logged a diagnosis: the honeypot rule must be skipping ordinary fields named website or url. We narrowed the rule. Nothing changed.
